source.title: The Alternative Growth Path
source.summary: Synthesis: what an Islamic growth model would look like, what's proven, what's speculative, and the research agenda ahead.
source.author: Islamic Economics
source.body_text: If you change the preference axioms, what growth path emerges? This episode brings together everything from the series: different savings behavior, equity-based investment allocation, intrinsically motivated labor, knowledge-driven institutions, and accountable governance. The theoretical prediction: potentially slower but more stable growth, more equitably distributed, with fewer boom-bust cycles and less financialization. But how much of this is proven? Very little. No country has implemented a comprehensive Islamic economic system. The wahn thesis is theoretically elegant but empirically untested. We're at the "interesting hypothesis" stage, not the "proven theory" stage. This episode maps the research agenda: formalize the preference axioms, find natural experiments, study Islamic finance's actual impact on allocation, measure zakat effects at scale, and build computable models. Islamic economics isn't claiming to have all the answers. It's asking different questions. That's scientifically legitimate.

x.single_post: Medieval Islamic scholars built universities while Europe burned books. Modern economists assume people maximize wealth. The research question is simple: what growth path emerges when your axioms include contentment and justice.
